---
title: "Why use a surrogate?"
---

Scientific simulators can be expensive to run. Tasks such as parameter fitting,
sensitivity analysis and interactive dashboards may need thousands of runs,
while one detailed agent-based simulation can take hours or days
[@chopra2023differentiableagentbasedepidemiology].

A **surrogate** learns to approximate a simulator from a bank of completed
runs. Once trained, it can produce new predictions much faster.

## Where METIS fits

METIS provides four neural surrogate models and the tools to train, compare
and save them. You bring simulator inputs and output trajectories; METIS helps
you turn them into a reusable model through Python or Hydra.

The usual workflow is:

1. Prepare a bank covering the inputs you care about.
2. Train on part of the bank.
3. Compare predictions with simulations the model has not seen.
4. Save the surrogate and use it for new inputs.

A fast surrogate is useful only if it reproduces the quantities your study
needs. Check errors, stochastic variation and physical constraints before
using it for decisions or inference. The
[model comparison guide](../package/model-choice.qmd) shows where to start;
SMRS provides a broader reporting standard [@NEURIPS2025_3e1d8e89].

Start with the [quickstart](../package/quickstart.qmd), or meet the
[SIRDS simulator](sirds-example.qmd) used in the examples.

::: {.callout-tip title="New to neural networks?"}
Basic Python is enough to run the examples. For background, try
[3Blue1Brown's introduction](https://youtu.be/aircAruvnKk) or the freely available
[Understanding Deep Learning](https://udlbook.github.io/udlbook/) textbook.
:::
